Wildlife would be disturbed from the effects of noise, dust, and human activities during periods when blasting and heavy equipment operations are conducted at the project site. These effects are expected to produce minor impacts compared to those anticipated from near-total disruption of surface features within the proposed impoundment site. The long-term effects of the action would be elimination of the area's productivity relative to the annual production of terrestrial fauna that could be expected within approximately 370 acres of second growth mixed deciduous and coniferous forest.
Short-term construction impacts described for the proposed reservoir area would also apply generally to the approximately 40 acres of land outside the Bad Creek drainage intended for use as a construction yard. Clearing of the area and its planned use for spoil and fill would eliminate its use as wildlife habitat. Similarly, the area for construction staging and heavy equipment service yard would also be lost to wildlife production. Until vegetative cover was established, heavy rains and runoff from areas of exposed fill could drain into the Whitewater River above lower Whitewater Falls and create localized siltation and turbid water conditions downstream. Temporarily, water quality would be degraded. Similar results could be expected in the upper Whitewater River arm of Lake Jocassee. These potentially disruptive factors would decrease as intensive use of the construction yard phased out and as environmental rehabilitation efforts began. The Applicant's restoration plans are discussed in Subsection 4.2.
Long-term effects on wildlife at the construction yard site of about 40 acres would result from the Applicant's proposed landscaping activities, changed soil composition, and modified natural drainage patterns. The outcome could be a localized reduction in diversity of micro-habitats. Wildlife would be permanently excluded from an approximately 3.5 acre area designated as a tie station; however, the remaining acreage would support a progressively more complex community as the rehabilitated zone underwent plant succession. Eastern cottontail, woodchuck, and other small game and non-game species frequenting openings and woodland edges would be favored. Transition from grasses and forbs to shrubs and saplings with consequent increase in available browse would attract white-tailed deer to the site. Ruffed grouse would also frequent the area.
